title: The Altitude Skier
twist: In the Thirsty Hiker case 'the air is thin' was wrong. Here it is the right answer — and the body's fix takes days, not minutes, without any extra fitness.
briefing: Noor, 15, lives near the beach and flies to a ski resort at 9,000 feet. On the first evening she is out of breath after one flight of stairs, her heart is thumping while she sits, and she has a dull headache. By the fourth day the stairs are easy and she feels normal — even though she is no fitter than when she arrived.
question: What changed in four days — the mountain, or Noor?

clues.title: Breathless on the stairs
clues.text: One flight of stairs at the lodge leaves her puffing. At home she runs up three without noticing.
clues.shows: that the same effort costs far more breath up here

clues.title: Thumping while sitting
clues.text: Resting on the sofa her pulse is about 80. At home it is about 65.
clues.shows: the heart working harder even at rest

clues.title: Thin, cold air
clues.text: The resort sign says 9,000 ft. A water bottle she sealed at sea level has puffed up like a balloon.
clues.shows: that the air pressure here is lower, so each breath holds less oxygen

clues.title: Fine by day four
clues.text: Same stairs, same lodge: by day four she is not breathless, her resting pulse is back near 70, and the headache is gone.
clues.shows: the body adjusting over several days without any training

hypotheses.text: She is unfit from sitting on the plane.
hypotheses.flaw: One day of sitting does not undo fitness, and if it had, four days of skiing would not bring her pulse down to normal.

hypotheses.text: The air at 9,000 ft holds less oxygen per breath, so at first her lungs and heart work harder; over a few days her breathing deepens and her blood carries more oxygen, so her heart can slow down again.
The cold is making her breathless.
hypotheses.flaw: It is just as cold on day four, when she feels fine — and cold air does not raise your resting pulse on a warm sofa.

hypotheses.text: She is dehydrated from the flight.
hypotheses.flaw: A drink of water would fix dehydration in an hour, not four days, and it does not explain the puffed-up bottle.

prediction.prompt: Noor goes higher and higher — from sea level up to 12,000 ft — on the day she arrives. What happens to her breathing rate while resting?

second.question: After a few days at altitude, what happens to her resting heart rate?

concepts.label: thinner air, less oxygen
concepts.hint: What is different about the air up there?

concepts.label: the body needs oxygen
concepts.hint: What does every breath deliver less of?

concepts.label: lungs and heart work harder
concepts.hint: What is the quick fix the body uses on day one?

concepts.label: blood carries more oxygen
concepts.hint: What slower change over a few days lets her blood carry more oxygen?

concepts.label: adjusts over days
concepts.hint: What happened between day one and day four?

transfer.context: A soccer team from a sea-level city plays a match in a city at 7,000 ft the day they arrive. The players tire much faster than usual, even though the home team runs just as far.
options: The visiting team is less fit.
Each breath at 7,000 ft holds less oxygen; the visitors' bodies have not yet adjusted, while the home team's have.
They are nervous about the crowd.
transfer.retryHint: Same effort, far more breath needed, on day one — which of Noor's clues is that?
transfer.explanation: The visitors arrived the same day, so their bodies are still on the quick fix — breathing and pumping harder — and they tire fast. The home players have lived at 7,000 ft long enough to have the slower fixes in place: deeper breathing all the time and blood that carries more oxygen. That is why teams often arrive days early.

takeaway: Higher up, each breath holds less oxygen. The body has a quick fix (breathe and pump harder) and a slower fix over a few days (breathe deeper all the time and concentrate the blood's oxygen carriers). Building new red blood cells takes weeks longer.
